module.title: Status & Diff: Reading What Changed
module.summary: Read git status like a report instead of a wall of text, and learn the diff format you will meet in every code review for the rest of your life.

lessons.title: Anatomy of git status — and of a diff

body.p: You have typed `git status` a dozen times by now, and if you are like most beginners you have been skimming it. Every line of it is a precise answer to a precise question, and learning to read it — along with a diff — is most of what separates someone who *uses* Git from someone who is *nervous around* Git.

body.h: Status is a report with three shelves

body.p: `git status` sorts the interesting files in your project into three sections. Those sections are the three areas from Module 3, printed top to bottom.

body.analogy: Picture packing for a trip. **Changes to be committed** are the clothes already zipped into the suitcase. **Changes not staged for commit** are the clothes lying on the bed — chosen, but not packed. **Untracked files** are still in the wardrobe: Git has never packed them, doesn't know you want them, and will leave without them.

body.p: All three sections at once. Read it slowly:

body.code:
On branch main

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	modified:   README.md

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   todo.txt

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	scratch.txt

list: `On branch main` — where you are working. (Branches arrive in Module 5.)
**Changes to be committed** — the staging area. `README.md` is in the suitcase: commit now and this is what you get.
**Changes not staged for commit** — the working directory. `todo.txt` has edits Git can see but was never asked to pack.
**Untracked files** — `scratch.txt` is brand new. Git has never stored a version of it and will not put it in any commit until you `git add` it.
The lines in parentheses are the exact commands Git suggests for each section — but read them before you run them: one of them is not like the others.

body.warn: Two of those suggestions are safe: `git add` and `git restore --staged <file>` only move a change between shelves. `git restore <file>` — same word, no `--staged` — throws your edit away and puts the file back to the last version Git knows about. There is no undo for that, because Git never had a copy of what you deleted. Check for the `--staged` before you press Enter.

body.p: A file can appear in **two** sections at once. Stage it, then edit it again: the suitcase holds the shirt you packed, and the bed holds the newer version you have ironed since. (Module 3’s camera, if you prefer: the frame still holds the version you placed in it.)

body.h: The line that trips absolutely everybody up

body.p: Now take `README.md` back out of the suitcase and ask again. Both files sit under **Changes not staged for commit**, and Git signs off with a line that reads like a contradiction:

body.code: no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

body.p: It means: *"if you ran `git commit` this second, the commit would be empty."* **Changed is not the same as staged.** The clothes are all over the bed; the suitcase is empty. That line has confused more beginners than anything else Git prints.

body.tip: `git status` changes nothing. Ever. It is the one Git command you can run as often as you breathe, and the fastest way out of "what state am I in?"

body.h: A diff is a set of edit instructions

body.p: Status tells you *which* files changed, never *how*. That is `git diff`, and what it prints is a **unified diff** — the format used by every code-review tool, and by every programmer showing another what they changed. Learn it once, read it forever.

body.analogy: A diff is not a picture of the new file. It is a proofreader's marks on the old one: *cross out this line, write this one instead, and add that one at the end.* The unmarked lines are printed too, quietly, only so you can tell where on the page you are.

body.p: Here is the diff of that `todo.txt` edit:

body.code:
diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt
index 88c4e99..525fdba 100644
--- a/todo.txt
+++ b/todo.txt
@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@
 - book the train
-- pack chargers
+- pack chargers (2x USB-C)
 - print tickets
 - water the plants
+- ask Sam to feed the cat

body.p: A header block, then the lines. Every part of it, once, so that none of it is ever mysterious again:

list: `diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt` — the header. **a/** is the *before* version, **b/** the *after*: same file, two moments in time.
`index 88c4e99..525fdba 100644` — internal ids and file permissions. Ignore this line for the rest of your career.
`--- a/todo.txt` and `+++ b/todo.txt` — which side is before (`---`) and which is after (`+++`).

`@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@` — a **hunk header**, and the only cryptic part. Read it as: *the before side contributes 4 lines starting at line 1; the after side contributes 5.* A **hunk** is one neighbourhood of edits plus three lines of context either side, so edits in two far-apart places print as two `@@` blocks with the untouched middle left out.

In real Git there is often text *after* the closing `@@`, like `@@ -40,7 +40,9 @@ def process_order(order):`. That is not part of the numbers — it is Git quoting the nearest heading above the hunk, so you can see where you are. This sandbox leaves it off.

Then the lines themselves: `-` was **removed**, `+` was **added**, a leading **space** is unchanged **context**. A reworded line shows up as a `-` and a `+` together, because Git compares whole lines, never words.

body.tip: Mnemonic: `-` is what **left**, `+` is what **arrived**. Changing one word in a sentence therefore costs you a whole `-` line and a whole `+` line.

body.h: The real question: which two things is it comparing?

body.p: This is where people quietly get lost, and it is the heart of the module. `git diff` has no single meaning: it has a *pair of endpoints*, and the flag you use chooses them. Your file can live in three places — the last commit, the staging area, your working directory — so there are three interesting gaps between them. (`HEAD` is Git’s name for the commit you are sitting on right now.)

body.analogy: Back to the suitcase. `git diff` holds the bed up against the suitcase: *what have I chosen but not packed?* `git diff --staged` holds the suitcase up against the packing list you filed last trip: *what will this trip's list say?* And `git diff HEAD` ignores the suitcase entirely, comparing the whole room against that list.

body.p: Each row of the table reads older on the left, newer on the right — the direction `add` and `commit` push your work into history, which is why the last commit sits at the far left:

body.code:
git diff            staging area -> working directory
git diff --staged   last commit  -> staging area
git diff HEAD       last commit  -> working directory
git diff <A> <B>    commit A     -> commit B

body.tip: `git diff --cached` in older tutorials and answers online is the same command — `--cached` and `--staged` are two names for one flag. Both work everywhere, including here.

body.p: There is no such thing as *the* diff. Ask two of those questions in the same second, about the same repository, and you can get two completely different answers — both correct.

body.warn: Every form of `git diff` is blind to **untracked** files. `scratch.txt` appears in no diff at all, because Git has no earlier version of it to compare against. It becomes visible — to `git diff --staged` — once you `git add` it, and then it arrives as `new file mode` over `--- /dev/null` (Git saying "before, there was nothing") with every line prefixed `+`.

body.h: Looking backwards: one commit, or the gap between two

body.p: Everything so far compares the present against something. You can also point Git at the past — at one commit alone, or at the gap between two.

graph.caption: Four commits. `git show <ref>` opens one dot and prints what it changed. `git diff <A> <B>` measures the distance between two dots — it does not care how many commits sit in between.

ops.content:
- book the train
- print tickets
- pack chargers
A tiny offline app for planning trips.

list: `git show HEAD` — the newest commit: id, author, date, message, **and** the full diff of what it changed. Plain `git show` means the same thing.

`git show HEAD~1` — one commit further back; `HEAD~2` is two back. You can also paste a short id from `git log --oneline` — the history you met in Module 2, squeezed to one line per commit: short id, then message.
`git diff HEAD~3 HEAD` — the net change across the last three commits as one diff. The steps in between disappear; you see only before and after.

body.p: `status`, `diff`, `show` and `log` are all **read-only**. None of them can lose an edit or change what you are about to commit. Prod at them as much as you like — that is the entire point of this module.

A café keeps its menu in Git. Someone edited `menu.txt` since the last commit and left a scratch file lying around, and nobody wrote down what they changed. You are going to find out — reading before you touch anything, then staging and committing once you know what you are agreeing to.
Watch for the moment in the middle where a change **vanishes** from `git diff`. That disappearance is the most useful thing in this module.

setup.content:
CORNER CAFE

SOUPS
- tomato
- lentil
- corn

SANDWICHES
- cheese
- hummus

DESSERTS
- apple pie
- ice cream

CORNER CAFE

SOUPS
- tomato
- lentil (vegan)
- corn

SANDWICHES
- cheese
- hummus

DESSERTS
- apple pie
- ice cream
- brownie

steps.say: Start where you always start. Read the report as three shelves: `menu.txt` is modified but **not staged**, `specials.txt` has never been committed at all, and the closing line tells you the suitcase is currently empty.

Status told you *which* file changed. Now ask *how*. You should see **two** `@@` hunks — one edit among the soups, one among the desserts — and nothing at all about `specials.txt`, because Git has no earlier version of it to compare against.
You have read the change and you approve of it. Put it in the suitcase.
steps.hint: Type: git add menu.txt — just that one file, not `git add .`, which would also sweep in specials.txt.

steps.say: Now run `git diff` again — and brace yourself, because you will get **nothing back**. Blank. That blank answer is the lesson: `git diff` only ever reports the gap between the staging area and your files, and you have just closed that gap. Nothing was lost.
steps.hint: Type: git diff again. An empty answer is the correct answer here.

steps.say: So where did the change go? One shelf to the left. `git diff --staged` compares the **last commit** with the **staging area** — in other words, it prints exactly what your next commit will contain. Same two hunks, different question.
Now make a second edit on top of the staged one — a new dessert — and look at status straight away. `menu.txt` is listed **twice**: the version you staged, and newer edits sitting on top of it.
steps.cmd:
echo "- lemon tart" >> menu.txt
git status
steps.hint: Two commands: echo "- lemon tart" >> menu.txt then git status

expect.label: menu.txt has a fresh edit on top

steps.say: Three questions, three answers. Right now `git diff` would show only the lemon tart, and `git diff --staged` would still show only the vegan lentils and the brownie. `git diff HEAD` skips over the staging area entirely and reports **everything** since the last commit. Run it and count the lines that begin with a single `+` — there should be three. (The `+++ b/menu.txt` header line is the after-side marker, not an added line.)

expect.label: See everything since the last commit

steps.say: You have read every change and you want all of it. Stage the newest edit too, then commit the lot.
steps.cmd:
git add menu.txt
git commit -m "Refresh the soups and desserts"
steps.hint: git add menu.txt, then git commit -m "Refresh the soups and desserts"

expect.label: Your commit records the menu.txt changes

steps.say: Last move: look backwards. `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD` asks for the *distance between two dots* — the commit before yours, and yours. Then open the commit itself: `git show` prints it from the inside, with its message, author and date above the very same diff. Run both and compare — the diff bodies are identical, and the only difference is the commit header on top.
steps.cmd:
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD
git show
steps.hint: Two commands: git diff HEAD~1 HEAD then git show

expect.label: Open the commit itself with git show

lessons.title: Challenge: find the change nobody mentioned

body.p: The pancake recipe has been through four commits and it no longer works — the pancakes come out flat. Nobody remembers editing anything they should not have.

Here is the thing about a good history: **every commit message is a promise about what that commit did.** Somewhere in these four commits, one of them quietly did something extra that its message never mentions. Find it with `git log`, `git show` and `git diff`, then undo only that.

setup.content:
Pancakes (serves 4)
- 2 eggs
- 1 cup flour
- 1 cup milk
- 1 tsp baking powder
- pinch of salt

Pancakes (serves 4)
- 4 eggs
- 1 cup flour
- 1 cup milk
- 1 tsp baking powder
- pinch of salt

setup.message: Double the eggs for a fluffier batter

setup.content:
Pancakes (serves 4)
- 4 eggs
- 1 cup flour
- 1 cup milk
- pinch of salt
- 2 tbsp sugar

setup.message: Sweeten the batter with a little sugar

setup.content:
Pancakes (serves 4)
- 4 eggs
- 1 cup flour
- 1 cup milk
- pinch of salt
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 1 tsp vanilla

exercise.goal: One of the four commits removed an ingredient without saying so. Work out which ingredient went missing, put that line back into `recipe.txt`, and commit the fix on its own. Every deliberate change — the extra eggs, the sugar, the vanilla — must survive. Finish with a clean working tree.
hints: Start with `git log --oneline`. Four commits, four promises. Now go and read what actually happened.
`git show HEAD~1` prints exactly what one commit changed. Walk back through the commits until you find the one whose diff removed a line its message never mentions.

`git diff HEAD~3 HEAD` compares the very first commit with the current one. Every difference in that diff should be explained by one of the four messages — except one. Look for a `-` line nobody promised.
To fix it, put the missing ingredient line back into the file (`echo "- 1 tsp baking powder" >> recipe.txt` works fine), then `git add recipe.txt` and `git commit -m "..."`.

expect.label: The missing ingredient is back in the committed recipe
The newest commit changes recipe.txt and nothing else

list: `git status` is a report with three shelves: **staged** (in the suitcase), **not staged** (on the bed), **untracked** (still in the wardrobe).
**no changes added to commit** means "committing right now would produce an empty commit". Changed is not staged.
A diff is a list of edit instructions: `-` left, `+` arrived, a leading space is unchanged context, and `@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@` tells you where in the file you are.
`git diff` never has one meaning — always ask *which two endpoints?*
`git show <ref>` opens a single commit; `git diff <A> <B>` measures the gap between two.
Untracked files are invisible to every form of `git diff` until you `git add` them.
`status`, `diff`, `show` and `log` are read-only — none of them can hurt you. The one command on this page that can is `git restore <file>` without `--staged`: it discards your edit for good.

body.code:
git diff            staging area -> working directory
git diff --staged   last commit  -> staging area
git diff HEAD       last commit  -> working directory
git diff <A> <B>    commit A     -> commit B

graph.caption: A history you can now interrogate: `git show` any dot, `git diff` between any two.

body.p: Next: branches — how to try an idea in a parallel universe without touching the timeline everyone else is standing on.

m4l3: git commit -m "Restore the baking powder dropped in the sugar commit"
